name: Hematological Disease Associated with an Acquired Peripheral Neuropathy

criteria.description: Detection of monoclonal gammopathy in serum or urine electrophoresis
Clinical signs and symptoms consistent with acquired peripheral neuropathy (sensory, motor, or sensorimotor)
Nerve conduction studies demonstrating demyelinating or axonal peripheral neuropathy
Exclusion of alternative causes of neuropathy such as diabetes, toxins, or hereditary neuropathies
Bone marrow biopsy or hematological workup supporting underlying hematological disorder

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of monoclonal gammopathy, clinical evidence of peripheral neuropathy, and electrophysiological confirmation
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis requires exclusion of other common causes of neuropathy and confirmation of hematological disorder.

searchTerms: nerve damage in hands and feet

pathognomonic.symptomName: Monoclonal gammopathy detected by serum protein electrophoresis
searchTerms: monoclonal protein found in blood test

common.symptomName: Numbness and paresthesia in distal extremities
searchTerms: numbness and tingling in hands and feet
abnormal feelings in fingers and toes

common.symptomName: Muscle weakness predominantly in distal limbs
Reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes

searchTerms: high levels of antibodies in blood
problems with automatic body functions including low blood pressure when standing
autonomic nervous system dysfunction causing dizziness

occasional.symptomName: Bone marrow plasmacytosis or lymphoplasmacytic infiltration
searchTerms: increased plasma cells in bone marrow
bone marrow with abnormal immune cells
excess plasma or lymph cells in marrow
mild anemia or low blood platelets

occasional.symptomName: Painful neuropathic symptoms (burning or shooting pain)

laboratory: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis showing monoclonal gammopathy
Elevated immunoglobulin M (IgM), IgG, or IgA depending on subtype
Bone marrow biopsy showing clonal plasma cells or lymphoplasmacytic infiltration
imaging: Nerve conduction studies demonstrating demyelination or axonal loss
MRI may show nerve root or plexus enlargement in some cases
genetic: No specific genetic mutations identified; typically acquired disorder
other: CSF analysis may show elevated protein without pleocytosis
Skin biopsy may reveal vasculitic changes in rare cases

redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness with respiratory compromise
Presence of systemic symptoms such as unexplained weight loss or night sweats
references: Dispenzieri A, Kyle RA. Paraproteinemic neuropathies. Neurol Clin. 2013;31(2): 491-505.
